title: Μελάνθιος καὶ κύων Ἄργος
titleEn: Melanthius and the Dog Argus — Odyssey 17.204–305
source: Homer, The Odyssey, Greek text of A. T. Murray (Loeb Classical Library; London: Heinemann, New York: Putnam, 1919), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg002.perseus-grc2, sha256 7d7ffafb6c51f8c2. Text as printed: Murray sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Odysseus, still disguised as a beggar, and Eumaeus come up the rough road to the town and reach the built spring with its grove and its altar of the nymphs. There they meet Melanthius, driving goats for the suitors' meal. He abuses the swineherd for bringing a beggar, threatens the stranger with flying footstools and kicks him on the hip; Odysseus considers killing him and holds back. Eumaeus prays to the nymphs for his master's return, and Melanthius answers with a wish for Telemachus's death and goes ahead to the hall. When the two arrive, Odysseus admires his own house as a stranger would, and they agree that Eumaeus will go in first. In the dung before the door an old dog, Argus, whom Odysseus reared before leaving for Troy, lifts his head, wags his tail and cannot come near his master; Odysseus wipes away a tear unseen and begins to question Eumaeus.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ στείχοντες ὁδὸν κάτα παιπαλόεσσαν
ἄστεος ἐγγὺς ἔσαν καὶ ἐπὶ κρήνην ἀφίκοντο
τυκτὴν καλλίροον, ὅθεν ὑδρεύοντο πολῖται,
τὴν ποίησ’ Ἴθακος καὶ Νήριτος ἠδὲ Πολύκτωρ·
sentences.tr:
all’ hote dē steichontes hodon kata paipaloessan
asteos engys esan kai epi krēnēn aphikonto
tyktēn kalliroon, hothen hydreuonto politai,
tēn poiēs’ Ithakos kai Nēritos ēde Polyktōr·
sentences.l:
But when indeed, going along the rugged road,
near the town they were, and to a spring they came,
wrought, fair-flowing, from which the townsmen drew water,
which Ithacus and Neritus and Polyctor made;
sentences.i: But when, making their way along the rugged road, they were near the town and had come to a built, fair-flowing spring, from which the townspeople drew their water, the spring that Ithacus and Neritus and Polyctor had made;
sentences.n: The sentence runs through four lines to the makers of the spring. ὁδὸν κάτα is κατὰ ὁδόν with the preposition set after its noun (anastrophe): 'along the road'. παιπαλόεσσαν is traditionally 'rugged', though its exact sense is uncertain. ἄστεος is the genitive of ἄστυ in the Homeric form (Attic ἄστεως), and ἔσαν is the epic ἦσαν. τυκτήν comes from τεύχω 'make, build': the spring is built, not natural. ὅθεν ὑδρεύοντο, with the suffix -θεν 'from where', has the middle of ὑδρεύω 'draw water', in the imperfect: it was where the townsmen used to draw. ποίησ’ is ἐποίησε with the augment dropped and the vowel elided. Ἴθακος is a man's name built on the same stem as the island's, Ἰθάκη.

sentences.t:
ἀμφὶ δ’ ἄρ’ αἰγείρων ὑδατοτρεφέων ἦν ἄλσος,
πάντοσε κυκλοτερές, κατὰ δὲ ψυχρὸν ῥέεν ὕδωρ
ὑψόθεν ἐκ πέτρης·
sentences.tr:
amphi d’ ar’ aigeirōn hydatotrepheōn ēn alsos,
pantose kykloteres, kata de psychron rheen hydōr
hypsothen ek petrēs·
sentences.i: All around it stood a grove of water-fed poplars, circular on every side, and cold water ran down from the rock above;
sentences.n: ἀμφί is an adverb here, 'around'. αἰγείρων is the genitive plural of αἴγειρος 'black poplar', depending on ἄλσος 'grove', and ὑδατοτρεφέων 'nourished by water' agrees with it, with the uncontracted ending -έων (Attic -ῶν). κυκλοτερές 'circular' is neuter, agreeing with ἄλσος. κατὰ … ῥέεν is tmesis: the preverb stands apart from the verb, which is an unaugmented, uncontracted imperfect, 'ran down'. ὑψόθεν has the suffix -θεν 'from': 'from on high'.

sentences.t:
βωμὸς δ’ ἐφύπερθε τέτυκτο
νυμφάων, ὅθι πάντες ἐπιρρέζεσκον ὁδῖται·
sentences.tr:
bōmos d’ ephyperthe tetykto
nymphaōn, hothi pantes epirrezeskon hoditai·
sentences.l:
and an altar above had been made
of nymphs, where all wayfarers used to sacrifice;
sentences.i: and above it an altar of the nymphs had been built, where every traveller used to offer sacrifice;
sentences.n: τέτυκτο is the pluperfect passive of τεύχω 'make', the verb behind τυκτήν four lines earlier. νυμφάων is the uncontracted genitive plural of νύμφη (Attic νυμφῶν), 'of the nymphs', the spring's divinities. ἐπιρρέζεσκον has the iterative suffix -σκ-: Homer adds it to a past tense to say that something happened again and again, 'used to'. ῥέζω is 'do', and of rites 'sacrifice'. ὁδῖται is 'travellers', from ὁδός 'road'. ἐφύπερθε is 'above'.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα σφέας ἐκίχαν’ υἱὸς Δολίοιο Μελανθεὺς
αἶγας ἄγων, αἳ πᾶσι μετέπρεπον αἰπολίοισι,
δεῖπνον μνηστήρεσσι·
sentences.tr:
entha spheas ekichan’ huios Dolioio Melantheus
aigas agōn, hai pasi meteprepon aipolioisi,
deipnon mnēstēressi·
sentences.i: There the son of Dolius, Melanthius, met them, driving goats that were outstanding among all the herds of goats, to be a meal for the suitors;
sentences.n: The Greek names the herdsman Μελανθεύς here; at 247 he is Μελάνθιος. They are two forms of one name, and the English gives Melanthius both times. σφέας is 'them', the epic accusative plural, and ἐκίχαν’ is ἐκίχανε, the imperfect of κιχάνω 'come upon, meet', with the final vowel elided. Δολίοιο is a genitive in -οιο (Attic Δολίου). αἳ … μετέπρεπον takes the dative: 'stood out among', and αἰπολίοισι is the dative plural in -οισι of αἰπόλιον 'herd of goats'. δεῖπνον μνηστήρεσσι is a phrase in apposition to αἶγας: the goats are a meal for the suitors; μνηστήρεσσι has the long dative ending -εσσι.

sentences.t: δύω δ’ ἅμ’ ἕποντο νομῆες.
sentences.tr: dyō d’ ham’ heponto nomēes.
sentences.l: and two herdsmen followed along with him.
sentences.i: Two herdsmen followed along with him.
sentences.n: δύω is the epic form of δύο 'two'. ἕποντο is an unaugmented imperfect middle of ἕπομαι 'follow'. νομῆες 'herdsmen' is the plural of νομεύς, built on νομός 'pasture'; the two are not named and say nothing in this part.

sentences.t:
τοὺς δὲ ἰδὼν νείκεσσεν ἔπος τ’ ἔφατ’ ἔκ τ’ ὀνόμαζεν,
ἔκπαγλον καὶ ἀεικές·
sentences.tr:
tous de idōn neikessen epos t’ ephat’ ek t’ onomazen,
ekpaglon kai aeikes·
sentences.l:
And them seeing, he reviled them and spoke a word and called them by name,
terrifying and unseemly;
sentences.i: When he saw them he reviled them, and spoke, calling them by name, in a terrifying and unseemly way;
sentences.n: τοὺς δὲ ἰδών: τούς is the pronoun 'them', the swineherd and the beggar. νείκεσσεν is the unaugmented aorist of νεικέω 'quarrel with, revile'. ἔπος τ’ ἔφατ’ ἔκ τ’ ὀνόμαζεν is a stock speech-introduction, 'spoke a word and called by name' (ἔκ … ὀνόμαζεν is tmesis, with ἐκ standing apart from its verb), and it can be used where the words that follow are hostile. ἔκπαγλον καὶ ἀεικές are neuter accusatives, 'terrifying and unseemly'; they may be taken with ἔπος or as adverbs, and the English takes them as adverbs.

sentences.t: ὄρινε δὲ κῆρ Ὀδυσῆος·
sentences.tr: orine de kēr Odysēos·
sentences.l: and he stirred the heart of Odysseus;
sentences.i: and he stirred the heart of Odysseus;
sentences.n: ὄρινε is the imperfect of ὀρίνω 'stir up, rouse', here with Melanthius as its unnamed subject and κῆρ 'heart' as its object. The Greek says no more of the effect than that Odysseus is moved; the next lines show the restraint that follows. Ὀδυσῆος has a single σ, a form Homer uses where the metre requires it.

sentences.t:
νῦν μὲν δὴ μάλα πάγχυ κακὸς κακὸν ἡγηλάζει,
ὡς αἰεὶ τὸν ὁμοῖον ἄγει θεὸς ὡς τὸν ὁμοῖον.
sentences.tr:
nyn men dē mala panchy kakos kakon hēgēlazei,
hōs aiei ton homoion agei theos hōs ton homoion.
sentences.l:
“Now indeed, quite utterly, a base man a base man is leading,
as always the like a god leads to the like.
sentences.i: “Now indeed, quite utterly, a base man is leading a base man, just as a god always brings like to like.
sentences.n: Melanthius, the speaker, turns a proverb into an insult. κακός means 'base' in worth and standing, not only 'bad'; the first κακός is Eumaeus, who leads, and κακόν is the beggar he leads. ἡγηλάζει is an uncommon verb, 'lead, guide'. The first ὡς is 'as', and the second, before τὸν ὁμοῖον, is the preposition ὡς 'to, toward' with an accusative of person. τὸν ὁμοῖον is an adjective used as a noun with the article, 'the like one'. θεός has no article: some god, unspecified.

sentences.t:
πῇ δὴ τόνδε μολοβρὸν ἄγεις, ἀμέγαρτε συβῶτα,
πτωχὸν ἀνιηρόν δαιτῶν ἀπολυμαντῆρα;
sentences.tr:
pēi dē tonde molobron ageis, amegarte sybōta,
ptōchon aniēron daitōn apolymantēra;
sentences.l:
Where, indeed, this scrounger are you leading, unenviable swineherd,
a beggar, irksome, a spoiler of feasts?
sentences.i: Where on earth are you leading this scrounger, luckless swineherd, an irksome beggar, a spoiler of feasts?
sentences.n: πῇ δή is 'where then?', with scorn. τόνδε is 'this one here', contemptuous. μολοβρός is a word of abuse whose meaning is not known: ancient guesses make it a 'glutton' or 'scrounger', and the English uses 'scrounger' only as a stand-in. ἀμέγαρτος is 'not to be envied', but its sense in use is uncertain; as an insult it comes to mean 'luckless', and the vocative ἀμέγαρτε is addressed to Eumaeus. ἀνιηρόν is 'irksome', from ἀνία 'distress, trouble'. ἀπολυμαντῆρα is a rare word, formed from λύμη 'ruin, outrage', and 'spoiler' is inferred from its parts. δαιτῶν is the genitive plural of δαίς 'feast'. συβῶτα is the vocative of συβώτης 'swineherd'.

sentences.t:
ὃς πολλῇς φλιῇσι παραστὰς θλίψεται ὤμους,
αἰτίζων ἀκόλους, οὐκ ἄορας οὐδὲ λέβητας·
sentences.tr:
hos pollēis phliēisi parastas thlipsetai ōmous,
aitizōn akolous, ouk aoras oude lebētas·
sentences.l:
who by many door-posts, standing beside, will chafe his shoulders,
begging for morsels, not swords nor cauldrons;
sentences.i: who, standing beside many door-posts, will chafe his shoulders as he begs for morsels, not for swords or cauldrons;
sentences.n: Here ὅς is the relative 'who', with the beggar as its antecedent. πολλῇς φλιῇσι is a dative plural in -ῇσι(ν): φλιή is a door-post, and παραστάς 'having stood beside' goes with it. θλίψεται is the future middle of θλίβω 'press, squeeze': he will rub his shoulders raw against the posts as he waits. αἰτίζων is 'begging'. ἀκόλους are 'morsels', scraps of food. οὐκ ἄορας οὐδὲ λέβητας, 'not swords nor cauldrons', sets what he will ask for against the gifts that men of standing give and receive; ἄορ is 'sword' and λέβης 'cauldron'.

sentences.t:
τόν κ’ εἴ μοι δοίης σταθμῶν ῥυτῆρα γενέσθαι
σηκοκόρον τ’ ἔμεναι θαλλόν τ’ ἐρίφοισι φορῆναι,
καί κεν ὀρὸν πίνων μεγάλην ἐπιγουνίδα θεῖτο.
sentences.tr:
ton k’ ei moi doiēs stathmōn rhytēra genesthai
sēkokoron t’ emenai thallon t’ eriphoisi phorēnai,
kai ken oron pinōn megalēn epigounida theito.
sentences.l:
Him if you would give me, to become a protector of the steadings,
and a pen-sweeper to be, and to carry fodder to the kids,
even whey drinking he would put a great thigh on himself.
sentences.i: If you were to give him to me, to become a protector of my steadings, a sweeper of the pens, and a bringer of green fodder to the kids, then drinking whey he would put a big thigh on himself.
sentences.n: τόν is 'him', the beggar, object of δοίης; εἰ with the optative makes it remote, 'if you were to give'; the κε(ν) of καί κεν at 225 belongs to what would follow. The infinitives γενέσθαι, ἔμεναι and φορῆναι say what he would be for: ἔμεναι is the epic infinitive of εἰμί, and φορῆναι an epic infinitive of φορέω 'carry'. σηκοκόρος 'pen-sweeper' is made from σηκός 'pen' and the verb κορέω 'sweep'. θαλλός is a green shoot or leafy branch, fodder for the kids (ἐρίφοισι, dative plural). ἐπιγουνίς is the thigh above the knee, and θεῖτο the aorist optative middle of τίθημι: he would 'put on' a thigh, that is, grow stout on the whey. The joke is that the idler would do well out of light work.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἐπεὶ οὖν δὴ ἔργα κάκ’ ἔμμαθεν, οὐκ ἐθελήσει
ἔργον ἐποίχεσθαι, ἀλλὰ πτώσσων κατὰ δῆμον
βούλεται αἰτίζων βόσκειν ἣν γαστέρ’ ἄναλτον.
sentences.tr:
all’ epei oun dē erga kak’ emmathen, ouk ethelēsei
ergon epoichesthai, alla ptōssōn kata dēmon
bouletai aitizōn boskein hēn gaster’ analton.
sentences.l:
But since indeed evil deeds he has learned, he will not be willing
to go about work, but cowering throughout the land
he wants, begging, to feed his own insatiable belly.
sentences.i: But since he has learned evil deeds, he will not be willing to set his hand to work; he would rather cower his way through the land, begging, to feed his own insatiable belly.
sentences.n: ἔμμαθεν is ἔμαθεν, the aorist of μανθάνω 'learn', with the consonant doubled for the metre; κάκ’ is κακά with the final vowel elided. ἐποίχεσθαι is ἐπί + οἴχομαι, 'go about, set about', with ἔργον as its object. πτώσσων is 'cowering, crouching', the way a frightened animal or a beggar moves. δῆμος is 'land, countryside' here, as in the house renderings. ἣν γαστέρ’ has the possessive ὅς: 'his own belly', and it is not the relative. ἄναλτος 'insatiable' is the ancient explanation of a word whose derivation is not clear. Odysseus takes up this same belly at 286.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἔκ τοι ἐρέω, τὸ δὲ καὶ τετελεσμένον ἔσται·
sentences.tr: all’ ek toi ereō, to de kai tetelesmenon estai·
sentences.l: But I will speak out plainly to you, and this too shall be a thing fulfilled;
sentences.i: But I will tell you plainly, and this too will come true:
sentences.n: This line is word for word 2.187. ἐκ … ἐρέω is tmesis for ἐξερέω, the future 'I will speak out'; τοι is the enclitic σοι 'to you'; τὸ δέ is 'and this', the article as a pronoun. τετελεσμένον ἔσται, 'will be a thing accomplished', is a future built from the perfect participle of τελέω, and it gives the sentence the ring of a prophecy: Melanthius makes his threat sound like an oracle.

sentences.t:
αἴ κ’ ἔλθῃ πρὸς δώματ’ Ὀδυσσῆος θείοιο,
πολλά οἱ ἀμφὶ κάρη σφέλα ἀνδρῶν ἐκ παλαμάων
πλευραὶ ἀποτρίψουσι δόμον κάτα βαλλομένοιο.
sentences.tr:
ai k’ elthēi pros dōmat’ Odyssēos theioio,
polla hoi amphi karē sphela andrōn ek palamaōn
pleurai apotripsousi domon kata ballomenoio.
sentences.l:
If he comes to the halls of divine Odysseus,
many footstools about his head, from the hands of men,
his ribs will wear away, as he is pelted through the house.”
sentences.i: If he comes to the halls of divine Odysseus, many a footstool flung about his head by men's hands will be worn away on his ribs, as he is pelted through the house.”
sentences.n: Read the syntax from the end: πλευραί 'ribs' is the subject and σφέλα, neuter plural 'footstools', the object of ἀποτρίψουσι, 'will rub away': the stools thrown at him will be worn out on his ribs. αἴ κ’ ἔλθῃ is 'if ever he comes', with εἰ and κε(ν) and the subjunctive. Ὀδυσσῆος θείοιο is a genitive in -οιο, and θεῖος is 'divine' in the house rendering. οἱ is 'on him', ἀμφὶ κάρη 'about his head', and ἐκ παλαμάων 'from hands' has the uncontracted ending (Attic παλαμῶν). βαλλομένοιο is a genitive participle, 'of him as he is pelted', naming the same man as οἱ. δόμον κάτα is κατὰ δόμον with the preposition after its noun.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτο, καὶ παριὼν λὰξ ἔνθορεν ἀφραδίῃσιν
ἰσχίῳ·
sentences.tr:
hōs phato, kai pariōn lax enthoren aphradiēisin
ischiōi·
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and passing by, with his heel he leapt in his follies
upon his hip;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and as he passed he kicked him on the hip, in his folly;
sentences.n: ὣς φάτο is the speech-closing 'So he spoke'. παριών is 'passing by'. λάξ is an adverb, 'with the heel', and ἔνθορεν the unaugmented aorist of ἐνθρῴσκω 'leap upon': he leapt at him with his heel, that is, he kicked him. ἀφραδίῃσιν is a dative plural in -ῃσιν, plural for the abstract 'folly'; the word is from ἀ- and φράζομαι 'consider', so 'thoughtlessness'. ἰσχίῳ is the hip. The Greek leaves the victim unnamed; he is Odysseus.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ μιν ἐκτὸς ἀταρπιτοῦ ἐστυφέλιξεν,
ἀλλ’ ἔμεν’ ἀσφαλέως·
sentences.tr:
oude min ektos atarpitou estyphelixen,
all’ emen’ asphaleōs·
sentences.l:
but not him out of the footpath did he thrust roughly,
but he stayed firmly;
sentences.i: and he did not shove him off the footpath, but stood firm;
sentences.n: οὐδέ … ἀλλά is 'not … but'. μιν is 'him', ἐκτός with the genitive ἀταρπιτοῦ 'out of the footpath'. ἐστυφέλιξεν is the augmented aorist of στυφελίζω 'strike hard, thrust'; the English keeps 'roughly' in the Greek-order line to link it with the verb's other use. ἔμεν’ is ἔμενε, the imperfect of μένω, elided, and ἀσφαλέως is 'firmly, without slipping'. The subjects are not named: Melanthius fails to move him, and Odysseus holds his ground.

sentences.t:
ὁ δὲ μερμήριξεν Ὀδυσσεὺς
ἠὲ μεταΐξας ῥοπάλῳ ἐκ θυμὸν ἕλοιτο,
ἦ πρὸς γῆν ἐλάσειε κάρη ἀμφουδὶς ἀείρας.
sentences.tr:
ho de mermērixen Odysseus
ēe metaïxas rhopalōi ek thymon heloito,
ē pros gēn elaseie karē amphoudis aeiras.
sentences.l:
but Odysseus pondered
whether, rushing after him, with a club he should take his life out,
or toward the ground should drive his head, lifting him bodily.
sentences.i: but Odysseus debated whether to rush at him and take his life out of him with a club, or to lift him bodily and drive his head to the ground.
sentences.n: ὁ δὲ μερμήριξεν Ὀδυσσεύς introduces a debate in the mind, and the two alternatives follow as ἠέ … ἦ with optatives (ἕλοιτο, ἐλάσειε), 'whether he should … or …'. μεταΐξας is the aorist participle of μεταΐσσω 'rush after, at'. ἐκ θυμὸν ἕλοιτο is tmesis for ἐξέλοιτο: 'take his life out'. ῥοπάλῳ is a dative of means, 'with a club'. ἀμφουδίς is a rare word whose sense is uncertain; 'bodily' is the traditional guess, and it goes with ἀείρας 'lifting him'. Neither is done, as the next words show.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἐπετόλμησε, φρεσὶ δ’ ἔσχετο·
sentences.tr: all’ epetolmēse, phresi d’ escheto·
sentences.l: But he endured, and in his mind restrained himself;
sentences.i: But he steeled himself and held himself back;
sentences.n: ἐπετόλμησε is from ἐπιτολμάω 'steel oneself to bear', built on τόλμη 'daring, endurance' (cf. τολμήεις at 284). ἔσχετο is the aorist middle of ἔχω, 'held himself back'. φρεσί is the dative of φρένες, 'in his mind' (a seat of thought, not a literal place). The Greek gives no reason for his restraint.

sentences.t:
τὸν δὲ συβώτης
νείκεσ’ ἐσάντα ἰδών, μέγα δ’ εὔξατο χεῖρας ἀνασχών·
sentences.tr:
ton de sybōtēs
neikes’ esanta idōn, mega d’ euxato cheiras anaschōn·
sentences.l:
and him the swineherd
reviled, looking at him face to face, and loudly prayed, his hands raising;
sentences.i: but the swineherd, looking at him face to face, reviled him, and prayed aloud with his hands raised:
sentences.n: τόν is the pronoun 'him', Melanthius. ἐσάντα is an adverb, 'face to face'. νείκεσ’ is νείκεσε, elided, the same verb as νείκεσσεν at 215: the abuser is now himself reviled. εὔξατο is the aorist of εὔχομαι 'pray' (it can also mean 'boast'), and μέγα 'loudly'. ἀνασχών is the aorist participle of ἀνέχω 'hold up', and the raised hands are the posture of prayer. The prayer follows.

sentences.t:
νύμφαι κρηναῖαι, κοῦραι Διός, εἴ ποτ’ Ὀδυσσεὺς
ὔμμ’ ἐπὶ μηρί’ ἔκηε, καλύψας πίονι δημῷ,
ἀρνῶν ἠδ’ ἐρίφων, τόδε μοι κρηήνατ’ ἐέλδωρ,
sentences.tr:
nymphai krēnaiai, kourai Dios, ei pot’ Odysseus
ymm’ epi mēri’ ekēe, kalypsas pioni dēmōi,
arnōn ēd’ eriphōn, tode moi krēēnat’ eeldōr,
sentences.i: “Nymphs of the spring, daughters of Zeus, if ever Odysseus burned thigh-pieces for you, covering them with rich fat, the thigh-pieces of lambs and kids, grant me this wish,
sentences.n: Eumaeus prays to the nymphs of the spring at whose altar they stand (cf. 211). The prayer runs: the gods addressed, 'if ever' they have been served, then the request. κρηναῖαι is the adjective from κρήνη 'spring', and κοῦραι is κόραι 'daughters'. ὔμμ’ is ὔμμι(ν) 'for you', elided. ἐπὶ … ἔκηε is tmesis: 'burned upon' the altar, with ἔκηε the unaugmented past of καίω 'burn'. μηρία are the thigh-bones, wrapped in fat and burned for the gods; the genitives ἀρνῶν ἠδ’ ἐρίφων say from what animals. πίονι is 'rich' with δημῷ 'fat'. κρηήνατ’ is the aorist imperative of κραιαίνω 'accomplish', and ἐέλδωρ is 'wish, longing'. The man he prays for stands beside him, unrecognised. The sentence is long, so it is cut at this comma.

sentences.t: ὡς ἔλθοι μὲν κεῖνος ἀνήρ, ἀγάγοι δέ ἑ δαίμων·
sentences.tr: hōs elthoi men keinos anēr, agagoi de he daimōn·
sentences.l: that may come that man, and may lead him a power;
sentences.i: that that man may come, and that some power may lead him;
sentences.n: ὡς introduces the wish itself, 'that', with the optatives ἔλθοι and ἀγάγοι, the optative of wish. κεῖνος is ἐκεῖνος, Ionic, 'that man'. ἑ is the enclitic accusative 'him'. δαίμων is an unspecified divine power, the force that is credited with what befalls a man, 'some power'. μέν … δέ pairs the two wishes: may he come, and may a power lead him.

sentences.t:
τῷ κέ τοι ἀγλαΐας γε διασκεδάσειεν ἁπάσας,
τὰς νῦν ὑβρίζων φορέεις, ἀλαλήμενος αἰεὶ
ἄστυ κάτ’· αὐτὰρ μῆλα κακοὶ φθείρουσι νομῆες.
sentences.tr:
tōi ke toi aglaïas ge diaskedaseien hapasas,
tas nyn hybrizōn phoreeis, alalēmenos aiei
asty kat’· autar mēla kakoi phtheirousi nomēes.
sentences.l:
Then he would scatter all your splendours,
which now in insolence you carry, wandering always
through the town; but the flocks base herdsmen are ruining.”
sentences.i: Then he would scatter all those splendours of yours, which you carry about now in your insolence, forever roaming through the town; but base herdsmen are ruining the flocks.”
sentences.n: τῷ is the article used as an adverb, 'in that case, then', and κε(ν) with the optative διασκεδάσειεν gives the result of the wish. τοι is the enclitic σοι 'for you', and ἀγλαΐας 'splendours' are Melanthius's fine show. ὑβρίζων is from ὕβρις 'insolence'. ἀλαλήμενος is a perfect middle participle of ἀλάομαι 'wander', in its reduplicated form, and ἄστυ κάτ’ is κατὰ ἄστυ with the preposition set after its noun and elided: 'through the town'. φορέεις is 'carry, wear'. The last clause is a bitter contrast: while he swaggers, the flocks are being ruined by 'base herdsmen' (κακοὶ νομῆες), whom the Greek does not name; μῆλα is 'flocks' and has the usual force 'small livestock'.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε Μελάνθιος, αἰπόλος αἰγῶν·
sentences.tr: ton d’ aute proseeipe Melanthios, aipolos aigōn·
sentences.l: Him then in turn addressed Melanthius, the goatherd of goats:
sentences.i: Then Melanthius, the goatherd of the goats, spoke to him in turn:
sentences.n: This is the αὖτε reply-formula, 'in turn, again': the speaker gives his answer to what has just been said. Μελάνθιος is the form of the name here, where line 212 had Μελανθεύς. αἰπόλος αἰγῶν, 'goatherd of goats', says twice what he does: the pleonasm is a plain epic habit. The line does not show a hostile intent, but the speech that follows does.

sentences.t:
ὢ πόποι, οἷον ἔειπε κύων ὀλοφώϊα εἰδώς,
τόν ποτ’ ἐγὼν ἐπὶ νηὸς ἐϋσσέλμοιο μελαίνης
ἄξω τῆλ’ Ἰθάκης, ἵνα μοι βίοτον πολὺν ἄλφοι.
sentences.tr:
ō popoi, hoion eeipe kyōn olophōïa eidōs,
ton pot’ egōn epi nēos eÿsselmoio melainēs
axō tēl’ Ithakēs, hina moi bioton polyn alphoi.
sentences.l:
“Ah, what a thing he has said, the dog, knowing baneful wiles,
whom some day I on a well-benched black ship
will take far from Ithaca, so that a great livelihood he may bring me!
sentences.i: “Ah, what a thing he has said, this dog who knows baneful tricks — whom some day I will take far from Ithaca on a well-benched black ship, so that he may bring me in a great livelihood!
sentences.n: ὢ πόποι is a cry of surprise or indignation. οἷον is the exclamatory neuter 'what a thing', object of ἔειπε, the aorist of the verb that Attic writes εἶπε. κύων 'dog' is abuse; the word is for Eumaeus. ὀλοφώϊα is a neuter plural used as a noun, 'baneful tricks', and the exact formation of the word is disputed. τόν ποτ’ ἐγών: τόν is the relative 'whom', ἐγών the epic ἐγώ, ἄξω the future of ἄγω. ἐπὶ νηὸς means 'on board a ship', and ἐϋσσέλμοιο 'well-benched' goes with μελαίνης 'black'. τῆλ’ is τῆλε 'far', with the genitive Ἰθάκης. ἄλφοι is the aorist optative of ἀλφάνω 'bring in, earn': the threat is to sell Eumaeus abroad, with the 'livelihood' as the price.

sentences.t:
αἲ γὰρ Τηλέμαχον βάλοι ἀργυρότοξος Ἀπόλλων
σήμερον ἐν μεγάροις, ἢ ὑπὸ μνηστῆρσι δαμείη,
ὡς Ὀδυσῆΐ γε τηλοῦ ἀπώλετο νόστιμον ἦμαρ.
sentences.tr:
ai gar Tēlemachon baloi argyrotoxos Apollōn
sēmeron en megarois, ē hypo mnēstērsi dameiē,
hōs Odysēï ge tēlou apōleto nostimon ēmar.
sentences.l:
Would that Telemachus silver-bowed Apollo might strike
today in the halls, or that he might be subdued by the suitors,
as for Odysseus far away the homecoming day has perished.”
sentences.i: If only silver-bowed Apollo would strike Telemachus today in the halls, or he were overcome by the suitors, just as for Odysseus, far away, the day of his homecoming has been lost!”
sentences.n: αἲ γάρ with the optative is a wish, 'if only' (Attic εἴθε or εἰ γάρ). βάλοι is the aorist optative of βάλλω 'strike'; ἀργυρότοξος Ἀπόλλων is 'silver-bowed Apollo', the archer-god who brings sudden death. σήμερον is 'today'. δαμείη is the aorist passive optative of δάμνημι 'subdue, overpower', with ὑπὸ μνηστῆρσι 'at the hands of the suitors'. ὡς … γε is 'just as'. Ὀδυσῆΐ is a dative of disadvantage, 'for Odysseus', with τηλοῦ 'far away'; the subject of ἀπώλετο is νόστιμον ἦμαρ, the day of homecoming, which is the phrase of 1.9. For Melanthius the day has already perished, and Odysseus is within hearing as he says it.

sentences.t:
ὣς εἰπὼν τοὺς μὲν λίπεν αὐτοῦ ἦκα κιόντας,
αὐτὰρ ὁ βῆ, μάλα δ’ ὦκα δόμους ἵκανεν ἄνακτος.
sentences.tr:
hōs eipōn tous men lipen autou ēka kiontas,
autar ho bē, mala d’ ōka domous hikanen anaktos.
sentences.l:
So having spoken, them he left right there, going gently on,
but he went, and very quickly the halls of the lord reached.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and left them there, still going gently on, while he went off and very quickly reached the halls of the lord.
sentences.n: ὣς εἰπών is 'so having spoken'. λίπεν is the unaugmented aorist of λείπω. αὐτοῦ is here the adverb 'right there', not the genitive of αὐτός. ἦκα is 'gently, slowly', and κιόντας is the accusative plural participle of κίω 'go': Eumaeus and Odysseus go on at their slow pace. Here ὁ is 'he' (Melanthius), βῆ is the unaugmented aorist of βαίνω, and αὐτάρ is 'but, and'. δόμους is plural for one house. ἵκανεν is the imperfect of ἱκάνω 'reach'. ἄνακτος is the genitive of ἄναξ 'lord', and the master of the house is Odysseus himself, who is walking behind.

sentences.t:
αὐτίκα δ’ εἴσω ἴεν, μετὰ δὲ μνηστῆρσι καθῖζεν,
ἀντίον Εὐρυμάχου·
sentences.tr:
autika d’ eisō ien, meta de mnēstērsi kathizen,
antion Eurymachou·
sentences.l:
Forthwith inside he went, and among the suitors sat down,
opposite Eurymachus;
sentences.i: He went in at once and sat down among the suitors, opposite Eurymachus;
sentences.n: αὐτίκα is 'at once', and εἴσω 'inside'. ἴεν is the imperfect of εἶμι 'go' (Attic ᾔει). μετά with the dative is 'among'. καθῖζεν is the imperfect of καθίζω 'sit down'. ἀντίον with the genitive is 'opposite, facing'. Eurymachus is one of the suitors; the next unit says why Melanthius sits by him.

sentences.t: τὸν γὰρ φιλέεσκε μάλιστα.
sentences.tr: ton gar phileeske malista.
sentences.l: for him he used to hold dear most of all.
sentences.i: for he held him dearer than all the rest.
sentences.n: φιλέεσκε is an iterative imperfect of φιλέω 'love, hold dear', with the same suffix -σκ- as ἐπιρρέζεσκον at 211: it describes his habitual feeling. τόν is the pronoun 'him', Eurymachus, and γάρ gives the reason for the seat. The subject is Melanthius, and μάλιστα is 'most of all'.

sentences.t:
τῷ πάρα μὲν κρειῶν μοῖραν θέσαν οἳ πονέοντο,
σῖτον δ’ αἰδοίη ταμίη παρέθηκε φέρουσα
ἔδμεναι.
sentences.tr:
tōi para men kreiōn moiran thesan hoi poneonto,
siton d’ aidoiē tamiē parethēke pherousa
edmenai.
sentences.l:
Beside him a portion of meats they set, those who were working,
and bread a revered housekeeper set beside him, bringing it,
to eat.
sentences.i: Those who were at work set beside him a portion of the meats, and a revered housekeeper brought bread and set it beside him, to eat.
sentences.n: πάρα is παρά with the accent drawn back, 'beside', and τῷ is 'him', Melanthius, who has just sat down (the Greek does not name him again). κρειῶν is the genitive plural of κρέας 'meat' (Attic κρεῶν), partitive after μοῖραν 'portion'. θέσαν is the unaugmented aorist of τίθημι. οἳ πονέοντο is 'those who were at work' (πονέομαι, uncontracted), the household servants busy at the meal. The second line is the line of 1.139 and stands in a stock scene of a meal laid out: the housekeeper (ταμίη) brings σῖτον 'bread, food'. ἔδμεναι is the epic infinitive of ἔδω 'eat' (Attic ἐσθίειν), here of purpose.

sentences.t:
ἀγχίμολον δ’ Ὀδυσεὺς καὶ δῖος ὑφορβὸς
στήτην ἐρχομένω, περὶ δέ σφεας ἤλυθ’ ἰωὴ
φόρμιγγος γλαφυρῆς·
sentences.tr:
anchimolon d’ Odyseus kai dios hyphorbos
stētēn erchomenō, peri de spheas ēlyth’ iōē
phormingos glaphyrēs·
sentences.i: Close by, Odysseus and the heavenly swineherd came up and halted, and the sound of the hollow lyre came about them;
sentences.n: ἀγχίμολον is an adverb built on ἄγχι 'near' and the root of μολεῖν 'come': 'close by, soon after'. Here Ὀδυσεύς has a single σ, as the metre needs. στήτην is a dual aorist of ἵστημι, 'the two stood', and ἐρχομένω the matching dual participle 'coming': Odysseus and Eumaeus are the two. δῖος ὑφορβός is 'the heavenly swineherd', with ὑφορβός a second word for swineherd. σφεας is 'them', and ἰωή is 'sound, voice'. ἤλυθ’ is ἤλυθε, 'came', a past of ἔρχομαι with its final vowel elided. φόρμιγγος γλαφυρῆς is 'of the hollow lyre', the usual epithet.

sentences.t:
ἀνὰ γάρ σφισι βάλλετ’ ἀείδειν
Φήμιος·
sentences.tr:
ana gar sphisi ballet’ aeidein
Phēmios·
sentences.l:
for for them he was striking up, to sing,
Phemius;
sentences.i: for Phemius was beginning to sing for them;
sentences.n: Φήμιος is Phemius, the household singer. ἀνὰ … βάλλετ’ is tmesis for ἀνεβάλλετο, the imperfect middle of ἀναβάλλω, which is used of 'striking up' a song, and ἀείδειν 'to sing' completes it: 'was beginning to sing'. βάλλετ’ lacks the augment. σφισι is a dative of the third-person plural pronoun, 'for them', the suitors. The unit ends mid-line, at the stop after Φήμιος.

sentences.t: αὐτὰρ ὁ χειρὸς ἑλὼν προσέειπε συβώτην·
sentences.tr: autar ho cheiros helōn proseeipe sybōtēn·
sentences.l: and he, taking him by the hand, addressed the swineherd:
sentences.i: and Odysseus took the swineherd by the hand and spoke to him:
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ὁ introduces the new action, and ὁ is 'he', Odysseus. χειρός is a genitive of the part grasped: 'taking by the hand', with ἑλών the aorist participle of αἱρέω. προσέειπε is 'addressed', and συβώτην the accusative 'the swineherd'. The speech that follows is the first half of a short exchange between the two.

sentences.t:
Εὔμαι’, ἦ μάλα δὴ τάδε δώματα κάλ’ Ὀδυσῆος,
ῥεῖα δ’ ἀρίγνωτ’ ἐστὶ καὶ ἐν πολλοῖσιν ἰδέσθαι.
sentences.tr:
Eumai’, ē mala dē tade dōmata kal’ Odysēos,
rheia d’ arignōt’ esti kai en polloisin idesthai.
sentences.l:
“Eumaeus, truly indeed these are fine halls of Odysseus,
and easily recognisable they are, even among many, to look upon.
sentences.i: “Eumaeus, these are truly fine halls of Odysseus, and they are easily known, even among many, when they are seen.
sentences.n: Εὔμαι’ is the vocative Εὔμαιε with its final vowel elided. ἦ μάλα δή is 'truly indeed'. δώματα is plural for one house, as elsewhere. κάλ’ is καλά elided. ἀρίγνωτα (ἀρι- 'very' + γνωτός 'known') is neuter plural, with the singular verb ἐστί, which is the regular Greek habit. ῥεῖα is 'easily'. ἰδέσθαι is an infinitive of respect, 'as to seeing'. Odysseus speaks of his own house as a stranger would.

sentences.t:
ἐξ ἑτέρων ἕτερ’ ἐστίν, ἐπήσκηται δέ οἱ αὐλὴ
τοίχῳ καὶ θριγκοῖσι, θύραι δ’ εὐερκέες εἰσὶ
δικλίδες·
sentences.tr:
ex heterōn heter’ estin, epēskētai de hoi aulē
toichōi kai thrinkoisi, thyrai d’ euerkees eisi
diklides·
sentences.i: Part rises out of part, and its courtyard has been fitted out with a wall and copings, and the doors are well-secured, folding in two leaves;
sentences.n: ἐξ ἑτέρων ἕτερ’ ἐστίν is compressed: the usual sense is that part is built upon part, as in a house of many connected buildings, but the phrase is not fully certain. ἐπήσκηται is the perfect passive of ἐπασκέω 'fit out, work up', and οἱ is 'for it' (the house). The datives τοίχῳ καὶ θριγκοῖσι are 'with a wall and copings' (θριγκός is the coping or crowning course of a wall). αὐλή is the courtyard. εὐερκέες is from ἕρκος 'fence', so 'well-fenced' and here 'well-secured', and δικλίδες is 'with two leaves', 'folding', from δίς and κλίς, the leaf of a door.

sentences.t: οὐκ ἄν τίς μιν ἀνὴρ ὑπεροπλίσσαιτο.
sentences.tr: ouk an tis min anēr hyperoplissaito.
sentences.l: not could any man it overpower.
sentences.i: no man could overpower it.
sentences.n: οὐκ ἄν … ὑπεροπλίσσαιτο is a potential optative, 'could not'. ὑπεροπλίζομαι is a rare verb, 'overpower', and its sense is a little uncertain. μιν is 'it', the house. The unit begins mid-line, after the stop at δικλίδες, and ends at the full stop that closes the line.

sentences.t:
γιγνώσκω δ’ ὅτι πολλοὶ ἐν αὐτῷ δαῖτα τίθενται
ἄνδρες, ἐπεὶ κνίση μὲν ἀνήνοθεν, ἐν δέ τε φόρμιγξ
ἠπύει, ἣν ἄρα δαιτὶ θεοὶ ποίησαν ἑταίρην.
sentences.tr:
gignōskō d’ hoti polloi en autōi daita tithentai
andres, epei knisē men anēnothen, en de te phorminx
ēpyei, hēn ara daiti theoi poiēsan hetairēn.
sentences.l:
And I perceive that many in it a feast are holding,
men, since the smell of fat wells up, and in it the lyre
sounds, which for the feast the gods made a companion.”
sentences.i: And I can tell that many men are holding a feast in it, since the smell of fat is rising and the lyre is sounding inside, the lyre that the gods have made the companion of the feast.”
sentences.n: γιγνώσκω is 'I recognise', and ὅτι 'that'. ἐν αὐτῷ is 'in it', the house. δαῖτα τίθενται is 'are making a feast for themselves' (middle). κνίση is the smell of burning fat, and ἀνήνοθεν is a perfect form from a verb meaning 'well up, rise', with present sense. μὲν … δὲ contrasts the smell with the sound. ἠπύει is 'sounds out', from ἠπύω 'call aloud'. In ἣν ἄρα δαιτὶ θεοὶ ποίησαν ἑταίρην, ἥν is the relative 'which', agreeing with φόρμιγξ, and ἑταίρην is a second accusative: 'made it a companion'. δαιτί is a dative, 'for the feast'.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφης, Εὔμαιε συβῶτα·
sentences.tr: ton d’ apameibomenos prosephēs, Eumaie sybōta·
sentences.l: Him, answering, you addressed, Eumaeus the swineherd:
sentences.i: In answer you said to him, Eumaeus the swineherd:
sentences.n: The poet speaks to Eumaeus in the second person: προσέφης is 'you addressed'. ἀπαμειβόμενος is the participle of ἀπαμείβομαι 'answer'. The line is the same as 14.55, and Εὔμαιε συβῶτα is the vocative.

sentences.t: ῥεῖ’ ἔγνως, ἐπεὶ οὐδὲ τά τ’ ἄλλα πέρ ἐσσ’ ἀνοήμων.
sentences.tr: rhei’ egnōs, epei oude ta t’ alla per ess’ anoēmōn.
sentences.l: “Easily you recognised it, since not in other things either are you witless.
sentences.i: “You recognised it easily, since you are not witless in other things either.
sentences.n: ῥεῖ’ is ῥεῖα 'easily', the word Odysseus used at 265, and ἔγνως, the aorist of γιγνώσκω, answers his γιγνώσκω at 269. ἐσσ’ is ἐσσί, the epic second person singular of εἰμί (Attic εἶ), elided. οὐδὲ … πέρ is 'not even, not either'. τά τ’ ἄλλα is an adverbial accusative, 'in the other things'. ἀνοήμων is 'witless' (ἀ- + νοέω). He is complimenting his guest on being sharp.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἄγε δὴ φραζώμεθ’ ὅπως ἔσται τάδε ἔργα.
sentences.tr: all’ age dē phrazōmeth’ hopōs estai tade erga.
sentences.l: But come now, let us consider how these deeds shall be.
sentences.i: But come now, let us think out how these matters will go.
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἄγε δή is a call to action, 'come now'. φραζώμεθ’ is the aorist subjunctive middle of φράζομαι 'consider, plan', in the hortatory sense 'let us'. ὅπως with the future ἔσται is 'how it will be'. The two have to decide how to enter the hall; Eumaeus sets out two plans.

sentences.t:
ἠὲ σὺ πρῶτος ἔσελθε δόμους εὖ ναιετάοντας,
δύσεο δὲ μνηστῆρας, ἐγὼ δ’ ὑπολείψομαι αὐτοῦ·
sentences.tr:
ēe sy prōtos eselthe domous eu naietaontas,
dyseo de mnēstēras, egō d’ hypoleipsomai autou·
sentences.l:
Either you first enter the well-inhabited house,
and go in among the suitors, while I will stay behind here;
sentences.i: Either you go in first, into the well-inhabited house, and go in among the suitors, while I stay behind here;
sentences.n: ἠέ opens the first of two alternatives; the second is introduced at 277 by εἰ δέ. ἔσελθε is εἴσελθε, the aorist imperative of εἰσέρχομαι. δόμους εὖ ναιετάοντας is the usual line-end phrase, 'the well-inhabited house', with plural δόμους for one dwelling. δύσεο is the aorist imperative middle of δύω 'go into, enter', with an accusative of what is entered. ὑπολείψομαι is the future middle of ὑπολείπω 'stay behind', and αὐτοῦ is the adverb 'right here', as at 254.

sentences.t: εἰ δ’ ἐθέλεις, ἐπίμεινον, ἐγὼ δ’ εἶμι προπάροιθε·
sentences.tr: ei d’ etheleis, epimeinon, egō d’ eimi proparoithe·
sentences.l: but if you wish, wait, and I will go in front;
sentences.i: or, if you prefer, wait, and I will go ahead;
sentences.n: εἰ δέ gives the second alternative after ἠέ in 275: 'or if you wish'. ἐπίμεινον is the aorist imperative of ἐπιμένω 'wait, stay'. εἶμι is a present form with future sense, 'I shall go'. προπάροιθε is an adverb, 'in front, ahead'. Eumaeus leaves the choice to his guest.

sentences.t:
μηδὲ σὺ δηθύνειν, μή τίς σ’ ἔκτοσθε νοήσας
ἢ βάλῃ ἢ ἐλάσῃ·
sentences.tr:
mēde sy dēthynein, mē tis s’ ektosthe noēsas
ē balēi ē elasēi·
sentences.l:
And do not you linger, lest someone outside noticing you
strike you or drive you off;
sentences.i: And do not you hang about, for fear that someone outside sees you and strikes you or drives you off;
sentences.n: μηδὲ σὺ δηθύνειν has an infinitive with the force of a command, 'and you, do not linger'; the verb of bidding, ἄνωγα, comes in the next unit and may be taken with it. δηθύνω is 'linger', from δηθά 'for long'. μή τίς σ’ … ἢ βάλῃ ἢ ἐλάσῃ is a clause of fear with the subjunctive. νοήσας is the aorist participle of νοέω 'perceive', here 'catching sight of'. ἔκτοσθε is 'from outside'. βάλῃ is 'strike' (with a missile) and ἐλάσῃ 'drive off', both with σε understood.

sentences.t: τὰ δέ σε φράζεσθαι ἄνωγα.
sentences.tr: ta de se phrazesthai anōga.
sentences.l: and these things I bid you consider.”
sentences.i: These are the things I bid you consider.”
sentences.n: τὰ δέ is 'and these things', the article as a demonstrative, object of φράζεσθαι, the middle infinitive of the verb of 274. ἄνωγα 'I bid, I order' is an old perfect with present meaning. It stands last: the whole speech is an instruction, and the instruction ends on the verb of command.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα πολύτλας δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.tr: ton d’ ēmeibet’ epeita polytlas dios Odysseus·
sentences.l: Him then answered much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus:
sentences.i: Then much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus answered him:
sentences.n: This is the standing reply-formula, and the house renderings keep it fixed. ἠμείβετ’ is ἠμείβετο, the imperfect of ἀμείβομαι 'answer', and ἔπειτα is 'then'. πολύτλας 'much-enduring' and δῖος 'heavenly' are two standing epithets of Odysseus, and each is translated every time.

sentences.t: γιγνώσκω, φρονέω·
sentences.tr: gignōskō, phroneō·
sentences.l: “I know it, I understand;
sentences.i: “I see, I understand;
sentences.n: γιγνώσκω is 'I recognise, I see how it is', and φρονέω 'I am thinking, I have it in mind'; the two present verbs, with no connective, answer Eumaeus's instruction at 279. These words are the same as at 17.193, where Odysseus answers Eumaeus on the road, and the next unit repeats the rest of that line.

sentences.t: τά γε δὴ νοέοντι κελεύεις.
sentences.tr: ta ge dē noeonti keleueis.
sentences.l: these things, indeed, to one who perceives you bid.
sentences.i: you are giving these instructions to a man who understands.
sentences.n: τά γε δή is 'these things indeed'. νοέοντι is a dative participle of νοέω (Attic νοοῦντι), 'to one who perceives', uncontracted. κελεύεις is 'you bid': Eumaeus's orders are lost on no one. The line repeats 17.193 with the same words.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἔρχευ προπάροιθεν, ἐγὼ δ’ ὑπολείψομαι αὐτοῦ.
sentences.tr: all’ ercheu proparoithen, egō d’ hypoleipsomai autou.
sentences.l: But go in front, and I will stay behind here.
sentences.i: Go ahead of me, then, and I will stay behind here.
sentences.n: ἔρχευ is the Ionic form of the imperative ἔρχεο (Attic ἔρχου). Odysseus takes Eumaeus's second plan (277: ἐγὼ δ’ εἶμι προπάροιθε): Eumaeus goes ahead, and the guest stays outside. ὑπολείψομαι αὐτοῦ is the same phrase as at 276.

sentences.t: οὐ γάρ τι πληγέων ἀδαήμων οὐδὲ βολάων·
sentences.tr: ou gar ti plēgeōn adaēmōn oude bolaōn·
sentences.l: for not at all am I unacquainted with blows nor with throws;
sentences.i: for I am by no means a stranger to blows and flung missiles;
sentences.n: οὐ γάρ τι gives the reason for waiting outside: 'for not at all'. πληγέων is the genitive plural of πληγή 'blow' (Attic πληγῶν), and βολάων the genitive plural of βολή 'a throw, a thing thrown' (Attic βολῶν). ἀδαήμων (ἀ- + δαῆναι 'learn, know') takes the genitive: 'unacquainted with'. The litotes, 'not unacquainted', is dry understatement, borne out by the next line.

sentences.t:
τολμήεις μοι θυμός, ἐπεὶ κακὰ πολλὰ πέπονθα
κύμασι καὶ πολέμῳ· μετὰ καὶ τόδε τοῖσι γενέσθω·
sentences.tr:
tolmēeis moi thymos, epei kaka polla pepontha
kymasi kai polemōi· meta kai tode toisi genesthō·
sentences.l:
enduring is my heart, since many evils I have suffered
in waves and in war; among them let this too come to pass;
sentences.i: my heart is an enduring one, since I have suffered many evils on the waves and in war; let this too come to pass along with them;
sentences.n: τολμήεις is 'enduring', from τόλμη 'daring, endurance' (the root of ἐπετόλμησε at 238), and μοι is a dative of possession, 'my heart'. πέπονθα is the perfect of πάσχω 'suffer': he has suffered, and that stays with him. κύμασι is the dative plural of κῦμα 'wave', and πολέμῳ the dative 'in war'. μετὰ … γενέσθω is tmesis for μεταγενέσθω: 'let it come to be among'; καὶ τόδε is 'this too', the blows to come, and τοῖσι ‘them’ the evils on waves and in war. The same words close Odysseus’s speech to Calypso at 5.224.

sentences.t:
γαστέρα δ’ οὔ πως ἔστιν ἀποκρύψαι μεμαυῖαν,
οὐλομένην, ἣ πολλὰ κάκ’ ἀνθρώποισι δίδωσι,
τῆς ἕνεκεν καὶ νῆες ἐΰζυγοι ὁπλίζονται
πόντον ἐπ’ ἀτρύγετον, κακὰ δυσμενέεσσι φέρουσαι.
sentences.tr:
gastera d’ ou pōs estin apokrypsai memauian,
oulomenēn, hē polla kak’ anthrōpoisi didōsi,
tēs heneken kai nēes eÿzygoi hoplizontai
ponton ep’ atrygeton, kaka dysmeneessi pherousai.
sentences.l:
But a belly in no way is it possible to hide, eager,
ruinous, which many evils to men gives,
for whose sake even well-yoked ships are fitted out
over the unharvested open-sea, bringing evils to the ill-disposed.”
sentences.i: But there is no way to hide a belly that is so demanding, so ruinous; it gives men many evils, and for its sake even well-yoked ships are fitted out over the sea that yields no harvest, bringing evils to the ill-disposed.”
sentences.n: γαστέρα is the object of ἀποκρύψαι, and οὔ πως ἔστιν is 'there is in no way (a possibility)'. μεμαυῖαν is the feminine accusative perfect participle of μέμονα 'be eager, press', here the belly's urgency. οὐλομένην 'ruinous' is the participle of ὄλλυμι 'destroy', used as a curse-word: οὐλομένης γαστρός, the same words in the genitive, is found at 15.344. τῆς ἕνεκεν is 'for whose sake', with the preposition after its genitive. ἐΰζυγοι is 'well-yoked', a word for ships whose exact sense is uncertain. ὁπλίζονται is 'are fitted out'. πόντον ἐπ’ ἀτρύγετον is 'over the unharvested sea', where ἀτρύγετος is a word of unknown meaning, 'unharvested' being the ancient guess. δυσμενέεσσι is the dative plural of δυσμενής 'ill-disposed'.

sentences.t: ὣς οἱ μὲν τοιαῦτα πρὸς ἀλλήλους ἀγόρευον·
sentences.tr: hōs hoi men toiauta pros allēlous agoreuon·
sentences.l: So they, such things to one another were saying;
sentences.i: So they talked in this way with one another;
sentences.n: ὣς οἱ μὲν τοιαῦτα πρὸς ἀλλήλους ἀγόρευον is a stock line that closes a conversation and changes the scene; it stands at 17.166 as well. οἱ is 'they', the two men, and μέν looks forward to ἂν δὲ κύων 'but up got a dog'. ἀγόρευον is the imperfect of ἀγορεύω 'speak'.

sentences.t:
ἂν δὲ κύων κεφαλήν τε καὶ οὔατα κείμενος ἔσχεν,
Ἄργος, Ὀδυσσῆος ταλασίφρονος, ὅν ῥά ποτ’ αὐτὸς
θρέψε μέν, οὐδ’ ἀπόνητο, πάρος δ’ εἰς Ἴλιον ἱρὴν
ᾤχετο.
sentences.tr:
an de kyōn kephalēn te kai ouata keimenos eschen,
Argos, Odyssēos talasiphronos, hon rha pot’ autos
threpse men, oud’ aponēto, paros d’ eis Ilion hirēn
ōicheto.
sentences.l:
But up a dog, lying there, lifted his head and ears,
Argus, of enduring-minded Odysseus, whom he himself once
reared, but had no enjoyment of him, before to holy Ilios
he went.
sentences.i: But a dog, lying there, lifted up his head and ears: Argus, the dog of steadfast Odysseus, whom Odysseus himself had once reared, but had no enjoyment of him, for before that he went to holy Ilios.
sentences.n: ἂν … ἔσχεν is tmesis for ἀνέσχεν, the aorist of ἀνέχω 'hold up'. κείμενος is 'lying', and the dog is named only in the next line. The English writes Argus for the dog and Argos for the city; Ἄργος is the same word. κεφαλήν τε καὶ οὔατα is 'head and ears' (οὔατα, the uncontracted plural of οὖς). ταλασίφρονος is 'enduring-minded', a standing epithet of Odysseus. In ὅν ῥά ποτ’ αὐτός, ὅν is the relative 'whom', and αὐτός 'he himself'. θρέψε is the unaugmented aorist of τρέφω 'rear'. ἀπόνητο is the unaugmented aorist of ἀπονίναμαι 'have profit or joy of', so οὐδ’ ἀπόνητο is 'nor had he enjoyment of him'. πάρος is 'before'. ᾤχετο is the imperfect of οἴχομαι 'go off'. ἱρήν is the Ionic form of ἱερήν 'holy'.

sentences.t:
τὸν δὲ πάροιθεν ἀγίνεσκον νέοι ἄνδρες
αἶγας ἐπ’ ἀγροτέρας ἠδὲ πρόκας ἠδὲ λαγωούς·
sentences.tr:
ton de paroithen agineskon neoi andres
aigas ep’ agroteras ēde prokas ēde lagōous·
sentences.l:
Him, before this, used to lead young men
after wild goats and roe-deer and hares;
sentences.i: Before that, young men used to take him out after wild goats, roe-deer and hares;
sentences.n: τόν is 'him', the dog, and πάροιθεν is 'formerly'. ἀγίνεσκον has the iterative suffix -σκ-, as ἐπιρρέζεσκον at 211: 'used to lead'. The men took him out hunting, the game being αἶγας ἀγροτέρας 'wild goats' (ἀγρότερος 'of the field, wild'), πρόκας (πρόξ, a kind of deer; 'roe-deer' is the traditional guess) and λαγωούς 'hares'. Each is joined by ἠδέ 'and', and ἐπί with the accusative means 'in pursuit of'.

sentences.t:
δὴ τότε κεῖτ’ ἀπόθεστος ἀποιχομένοιο ἄνακτος,
ἐν πολλῇ κόπρῳ, ἥ οἱ προπάροιθε θυράων
ἡμιόνων τε βοῶν τε ἅλις κέχυτ’, ὄφρ’ ἂν ἄγοιεν
δμῶες Ὀδυσσῆος τέμενος μέγα κοπρήσοντες·
sentences.tr:
dē tote keit’ apothestos apoichomenoio anaktos,
en pollēi koprōi, hē hoi proparoithe thyraōn
hēmionōn te boōn te halis kechyt’, ophr’ an agoien
dmōes Odyssēos temenos mega koprēsontes·
sentences.l:
Then indeed he lay, neglected, his lord gone away,
in much dung, which before the doors
of mules and of cattle lay heaped in abundance, until might carry it
the slaves of Odysseus to the great precinct, to dung it;
sentences.i: Then, with his lord gone away, he lay neglected in much dung, the dung of mules and cattle that lay heaped in abundance before the doors, until the slaves of Odysseus should carry it off to manure his great estate;
sentences.n: δὴ τότε is 'then indeed', and κεῖτ’ is κεῖτο 'lay'. ἀπόθεστος is a rare word of uncertain sense; 'neglected' is the ancient guess. ἀποιχομένοιο ἄνακτος is a genitive absolute, 'his lord having gone away'. κόπρος is 'dung', with ἡμιόνων τε βοῶν τε 'of mules and of cattle'. ἥ is the relative, feminine, 'which', agreeing with κόπρῳ, and οἱ is the dative of the person concerned; κέχυτ’ is from χέω 'pour', so 'lay heaped'. ὄφρ’ ἂν ἄγοιεν is 'until they should carry' (ὄφρα with ἄν and the optative). τέμενος is land marked off for a chief or a god; the Greek-order line keeps 'precinct' as shipped at 6.293 and 8.363, the English line 'estate', since this is a chief's own farmland. κοπρήσοντες is a future participle of purpose, 'to manure'.

sentences.t: ἔνθα κύων κεῖτ’ Ἄργος, ἐνίπλειος κυνοραιστέων.
sentences.tr: entha kyōn keit’ Argos, enipleios kynoraisteōn.
sentences.l: There the dog lay, Argus, full of dog-ticks.
sentences.i: There the dog Argus lay, full of dog-ticks.
sentences.n: κεῖτ’ is κεῖτο again, the verb of 296, now with the dog's name. ἐνίπλειος 'full of' takes the genitive. κυνοραιστέων is the genitive plural of κυνοραιστής, the 'dog-tick' (κυνο- is 'dog'), with the uncontracted ending -έων (Attic -ῶν).

sentences.t:
δὴ τότε γ’, ὡς ἐνόησεν Ὀδυσσέα ἐγγὺς ἐόντα,
οὐρῇ μέν ῥ’ ὅ γ’ ἔσηνε καὶ οὔατα κάββαλεν ἄμφω,
ἆσσον δ’ οὐκέτ’ ἔπειτα δυνήσατο οἷο ἄνακτος
ἐλθέμεν·
sentences.tr:
dē tote g’, hōs enoēsen Odyssea engys eonta,
ourēi men rh’ ho g’ esēne kai ouata kabbalen amphō,
asson d’ ouket’ epeita dynēsato hoio anaktos
elthemen·
sentences.l:
Then indeed, when he perceived Odysseus nearby,
with his tail he, for his part, fawned, and his ears he dropped, both,
but nearer no longer then was he able of his own lord
to go;
sentences.i: Then, when he perceived that Odysseus was near, he fawned with his tail and dropped both his ears, but he was no longer able to come nearer to his own lord;
sentences.n: ὡς ἐνόησεν is 'when he perceived', the aorist of νοέω. ἐόντα is ὄντα, 'being'. οὐρῇ is the dative of οὐρά 'tail', and ἔσηνε the unaugmented aorist of σαίνω 'wag the tail, fawn'. ῥ’ is the particle ῥα, and ὅ γε 'he, for his part' is the dog. κάββαλεν is κατέβαλε, the augment lost and the consonant of κατ- assimilated to the next: 'dropped'. ἆσσον is the comparative adverb 'nearer', and οἷο ἄνακτος is the genitive of the possessive 'his own lord'. δυνήσατο is the aorist middle of δύναμαι 'be able'. ἐλθέμεν is the epic infinitive of ἔρχομαι.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὁ νόσφιν ἰδὼν ἀπομόρξατο δάκρυ,
ῥεῖα λαθὼν Εὔμαιον, ἄφαρ δ’ ἐρεείνετο μύθῳ·
sentences.tr:
autar ho nosphin idōn apomorxato dakry,
rheia lathōn Eumaion, aphar d’ ereeineto mythōi·
sentences.l:
but he, looking aside, wiped away a tear,
easily escaping the notice of Eumaeus, and straightway he questioned him with a word:
sentences.i: but Odysseus looked away and wiped away a tear, easily escaping Eumaeus's notice, and at once questioned him:
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ὁ is 'but he', Odysseus. νόσφιν is 'aside, apart', and with ἰδών it is 'looking away'. ἀπομόρξατο is the aorist middle of ἀπομόργνυμι 'wipe off': he wipes his own face. δάκρυ is the epic singular 'tear'. ῥεῖα is 'easily', as at 265 and 273, and λαθών is the aorist participle of λανθάνω 'escape the notice of', here with the accusative Εὔμαιον. ἄφαρ is 'at once'. ἐρεείνετο is the imperfect of ἐρεείνω 'ask, question', and μύθῳ is 'with a word'. The question itself falls after the end of this part.
